content: Human African trypanosomiasis, commonly known as sleeping sickness, is a severe and prolonged illness that primarily affects individuals in the most impoverished regions of Africa. Without treatment, the disease is invariably fatal. For the second stage of the disease, there are only a few drugs available, and these are associated with significant adverse effects and varying levels of efficacy. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness and safety of drugs used to treat second-stage human African trypanosomiasis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, BIOSIS, and mRCT, up to January 2013. Researchers and organizations working in this field were also contacted for additional information. The study included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials involving both adults and children diagnosed with second-stage human African trypanosomiasis and treated with anti-trypanosomal drugs. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed by two authors, with a third author serving as an arbitrator in cases of disagreement. The trials reported dichotomous outcomes, which were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of nine trials involving 2,577 participants, all infected with Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, were included in the analysis. Seven of these trials evaluated currently available drugs, including melarsoprol, eflornithine, and nifurtimox, either as monotherapies or in combination. One trial tested pentamidine, and another assessed the addition of prednisolone to melarsoprol. The results showed that the frequency of death and the number of adverse events were comparable between patients treated with a fixed 10-day regimen of melarsoprol and those treated with a 26-day regimen. However, melarsoprol monotherapy was associated with fewer relapses compared to pentamidine or nifurtimox, but it caused more adverse events. Later trials evaluated the combination of nifurtimox and eflornithine (NECT), which demonstrated fewer relapses and better tolerability. NECT also offered practical advantages, such as reducing the frequency and number of eflornithine infusions to twice daily, thereby alleviating the burden on healthcare providers and patients. The authors concluded that the choice of therapy for second-stage Gambiense human African trypanosomiasis will continue to depend on local availability of drugs. However, eflornithine and NECT are likely to replace melarsoprol as the preferred treatments, provided that parasite resistance is carefully monitored. Further research is needed to minimize the adverse effects of currently used drugs, explore alternative treatment regimens, and develop new compounds that are effective against both stages of the disease.
